newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Paris court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.

text.p: The French Supreme Court ordered former cabinet minister Maurice Papon on Thursday to stand trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deporting 1,690 Jews, including 223 children, to Nazi death camps in 1942-44.
The trial by jury in a Bordeaux assize court, following a legal marathon of more than 15 years, will probably be the last chance to put France's wartime collaboration with the Nazis in the dock.
In a last-ditch bid to avoid trial, Papon, 86, had appealed to the Supreme Court after the Bordeaux appeals court ruled last September that he should stand trial.
Public prosecutors have built up a 50,000-page case against Papon, who was secretary-general of the Bordeaux prefect's office under the collaborationist Vichy government.

In a statement issued minutes after the Supreme Court ruling, Papon branded the decision strange and scandalous, adding that it would allow Communists, "the leftist lobby", state authorities and foreign institutions trying to tie France to the Holocaust to settle old scores.
"As in all political trials, the outcome has already been settled with the authorities. I will resist such dishonouring acts which recall the sad adventure of Captain Dreyfus," Papon said.

French army officer Alfred Dreyfus, born to a Jewish family, was convicted of treason in 1884 on forged evidence and jailed. He was eventually declared innocent after a bitter controversy tinged with anti-semitism which deeply split the country.

His wartime record unknown, Papon enjoyed a meteoric post-war career, serving as Paris police chief in the 1960s and then as budget minister in the 1970s until files documenting his arrests and deportation orders were found in 1981.
After benefiting from delaying tactics by successive governments, Papon will be only the second Frenchman -- and probably the last -- to be sent to trial on such charges arising from the war.

A lower-ranking collaborationist, former militia officer Paul Touvier, was jailed for life in 1994 and died in prison last year aged 81. A former police chief in the Vichy government, Rene Bousquet, was shot dead by a publicity-hungry failed writer in 1993 before he could stand trial.

The Bordeaux appeals court sent Papon to a jury trial in an assize court on charges of being an accomplice to the kidnapping and murder of deportees sent to Nazi death camps. Few of the deportees ever returned.
The court also approved charges that Papon was an accomplice to arbitrary arrests, the arrest of minors under 15 years old, inhuman acts and attempted illegal arrests.

Prosecutors say the Holocaust was "one of the war's best-kept secrets" and that they have not managed to establish whether Papon knew the fate of the Jews he sent to Drancy in Paris, a transit camp for deportees to Nazi death camps.
Papon says he helped the Resistance, saved several Jews and watered down the harshest provisions made by the Vichy government.

In 1981, arrest warrants, chartering of trains and other orders bearing his signature were found. Legal proceedings began in 1983, were annulled on technicalities in 1987, started again from scratch and were finally completed in June 1995.
The late President Francois Mitterrand, himself a former Vichy official, sought to prevent trials for crimes against humanity because he said they undermined national unity.
His Gaullist successor Jacques Chirac acknowledged in 1995 French state responsibility in the deportation of the Jews, the first post-war leader to do so.
